title: Monica Bellucci Has ‘Never’ Done Anything Like ‘Ketticè’: ‘I Was on Set in My Pajamas With a Knife in My Hand and Slippers on My Feet’
description:
Do you think Monica Bellucci has done it all? Think again.

	“I’ve never done anything like that,” she tells Variety about her role in “Ketticè.” Di
body:
Do you think Monica Bellucci has done it all? Think again.

	“I’ve never done anything like that,” she tells Variety about her role in “Ketticè.” Directed by Giovanni Tortorici, the film premiered at Locarno. 

	“I was on set in my pajamas with a knife in my hand and slippers on my feet. This woman has abandoned her femininity.” 


	Set in Palermo in 2012, “Ketticè” follows teenage Giulio who becomes increasingly lost, even after his encounter with a spirited girl named Ketty. So does his mother. 
	

	“It was interesting to play this wife and mother who represents the angst and frustration behind the apparent perfection of decaying high society. She’s an unhappy woman, bitter, with a kind of rage, but she has no outlet for it.”

	As her character struggles to find balance, her relationship with her son brims with tension. 

	“She tries to counterbalance this frustration by eating little cakes and screaming constantly. Sometimes, the situation becomes almost comical. There is a real generational incomprehension between the two of them.”

	Throughout her career, Bellucci hasn’t done many comedies, though she has certainly proven her comedic timing in “Call My Agent!” or “Asterix & Obelix: Mission Cleopatra.”

	“I expressed my dark side more: in ‘Malèna,’ ‘Irréversible’ or ‘The Passion of the Christ.’ Then, I did many genre films, from James Bond to ‘Brotherhood of the Wolf’ or ‘Matrix’,” she recalls. But in “Ketticè,” her character is tragicomic at times.
	

	“She threatens her husband with a knife, but nobody’s scared of her. She screams, she’s aggressive, but everyone knows she won’t go anywhere. She wouldn’t have the courage to change her life. In the end, she’s their slave,” says the star. 

	Earlier this week, Tortorici told Variety that Bellucci delivered a “very intelligent, very realistic interpretation, even if the character is a bit eccentric. I have to say that when I showed the film to people who also know this aristocratic world, they told me that they found a lot of truth in her performance.”

	“Giovanni is young, but he’s completely in control of the set. He made a personal, unique movie,” reciprocates Bellucci, also praising young co-stars Salvatore Gallina and Rachele Testagrossa. “They brought these fully believable characters to life. When young people work like that, it means the director is talented.” 

	“Giovanni looks so calm and sweet, but on set, he was a tiger – in a good way!,” she laughs. 

	“He knew where he was going.”

	This year, Bellucci worked with many young directors, from Maria Sole Tognazzi to Léa Mysius’ (Cannes premiere “The Birthday Party”) and Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah (“Seven Dogs”). 

	“It’s interesting because there’s really an exchange, you know? They come with their own universe, point of view and excitement, and I come with my experience.”

	“Léa Mysius is a young director, but she’s already respected in France. She also gave me the opportunity to play a beautiful role unlike anything I’ve done before. It’s character far from my Mediterranean temperament. She wants to live in isolation, which is the opposite of who I am in life.”

	Bellucci continues to choose her roles “through instinct.”

	“When I worked with David Lynch [on ‘Twin Peaks’], I had just one scene. But sometimes, it really doesn’t matter if it’s a smaller role. I just like to be free,” she said. 

	“What I like about my work is the element of surprise. I like it when directors come to me with ideas I hadn’t thought of, even though I’ve been here for so many years. I still have the excitement and passion for my work.” 

	She adds: “Our bodies change, of course, but we can express other aspects of life that we couldn’t before. I could never have done ‘The Birthday Party’ when I was 30 or 40. I needed more experience to portray these kinds of emotions.”
	

	“Today, we actresses are so lucky to have the chance to keep working even as adult women. In the past, it was impossible to have a career after 40. It’s slow, but things are changing,” she says. 

	Still, it’s not all there is. 

	“I love what I do and I’m very grateful that I still have the chance to do interesting things. But life is more important,” she states. 

	“Life is stronger than art.”

schema.headline: Monica Bellucci Has ‘Never’ Done Anything Like ‘Ketticè’: ‘I Was on Set in My Pajamas With a Knife in My Hand and Slippers on My Feet’

title: George MacKay, Louisa Harland, Nathalie Emmanuel and Eric Kofi Abrefa Join ‘The Animals’ From ‘Supacell’ Star Calvin Demba (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Calvin Demba, the British actor, writer and director best known on screen for the Netflix hit “Supacell,” has lined up an impressive cast list for h
body:
Calvin Demba, the British actor, writer and director best known on screen for the Netflix hit “Supacell,” has lined up an impressive cast list for his second short film behind the camera, “The Animals.”

	George MacKay (“Rose of Nevada,” “Sense and Sensibility”) stars alongside Louisa Harland (“Renegade Nell,” “Derry Girls”), Nathalie Emmanuel (“Game of Thrones,” “Megalopolis”) and Eric Kofi Abrefa (“Supacell,” BMF”) in the project, written and directed by Demba and produced by Tuli Litvak (“Beauty Sleep,” “Fairview Park”).
	

	“The Animals” centers on Miles (MacKay) as he struggles with growing feelings of emasculation and emotional impotency within his relationship with Remona (Harland). An opportunity to reclaim his sense of self arises from another man’s act of heroism during a violent home invasion — but as events spiral out of control, he’s forced to confront the destructive masculine ideals driving him.


	“I wanted to make a film that takes a satirical look at gender stereotypes and the role they play in relationships,” said Demba, who made his directorial debut with 2022’s BFI Network short “BabyDolls.” “‘The Animals’ examines masculinity and how it can become performative. It pokes fun at modern relationships and the ways we unconsciously perform gender roles within them, exploring the gap between who we are and who we feel we should be. Tonally, the film is darkly comic, but the violence never feels slapstick. It needed to feel grounded in reality because that threat of violence mirrors the conversations we’re having about masculinity itself.”
	

	Added MacKay: “What drew me to the project was the script and the opportunity to work with Calvin. I’m a huge fan of his previous work and wanted to be part of whatever he made next. Working with Cal, and his mix of detail and freedom, was my favourite part of the process. His generosity as a writer and director, and his willingness to share that process, was golden.”

	“The Animals,” which was shot earlier this year, was filmed on 16mm by Ebba Hult (whose work has screened at Cannes, Telluride, and LFF), edited by Mdhamiri Á Nkemi (“The Last Tree,” “Blue Story”), and graded by Canadian colourist Jodie Davison (“The Revenant,” “The Eternal Daughter”). It is executive produced by BAFTA-winners Mouktar Mohammed (“Supacell”) and Sheila Nortley (“Supacell,” “Stay Close”), Demba and Harland.

	“This film was a total joy to make because we had such a clever script and such an incredible team, and I loved getting to work alongside George who I have long admired,” said Harland. “The script is what drew me to this role, but I really believe in Calvin as a filmmaker. His stories are rooted in poetry, and I hope to continue working with him on every project he does, whether that’s in front of or behind the camera.”

	“The Animals” will begin its festival circuit at a BAFTA and Oscar qualifying major festival, to be announced soon. Demba is currently in early development with the BFI to turn the short into a feature film.

schema.headline: George MacKay, Louisa Harland, Nathalie Emmanuel and Eric Kofi Abrefa Join ‘The Animals’ From ‘Supacell’ Star Calvin Demba (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Films Boutique Nabs Mani Haghighi’s ‘I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies’ Ahead of New York Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Berlin-based sales agency Films Boutique has acquired worldwide rights to Iranian filmmaker Mani Haghighi’s documentary “I Deserve a Lover Whose Eve
body:
Berlin-based sales agency Films Boutique has acquired worldwide rights to Iranian filmmaker Mani Haghighi’s documentary “I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies,” which is set to premiere at the New York Film Festival.

	Set between Tabriz and Tehran in the weeks between the 12-Day War and the subsequent U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran, the documentary accompanies two artists whose lives have become inseparable from a vast private archive assembled over decades: photographs, documents, discarded objects, and traces of anonymous lives.
	

	Working somewhere between collecting, hoarding, preservation and obsession, Nasser Bakhshi, a painter, conceptual artist, collector and curator, and his partner Roghayeh Najdi have created an improvised museum of neglected lives, one in which sex workers, young soldiers, child labourers and ordinary families emerge through abandoned albums, damaged belongings and fragments of memory left behind by history.


	“Their sprawling collection of found art objects has helped preserve Iran’s contemporary history as an artistic and political act,” reads the logline. Films Boutique describes “I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies” as Haghighi’s “most formally inventive and culturally urgent documentary feature to date.”

	“Mani’s new work blew us away, capturing the essence of collective preservation through a completely fresh artistic and cinematic approach,” Films Boutique CEO Jean-Christophe Simon told Variety. “Profiling a highly eccentric and deeply sympathetic couple of artists within a monumental archive, this film represents a profound exploration from an outstanding, fearless voice in world cinema, one that feels in dialogue with filmmakers from Bergman to Parajanov.
	

	“We cannot wait to launch its international journey starting with its prestigious world premiere at the New York Film Festival.” 

	Haghighi expressed delight at re-teaming with the company. “I am absolutely thrilled to be working with Films Boutique once again. Their passion for bold cinema and their incredible dedication to filmmakers make them the perfect home for this film.

	“I am delighted to put Nasser Bakhshi and Roghayeh Najdi’s incredible story in such able hands, and look forward to share, with the help of Films Boutique, this deeply personal film with global audiences.”

	Haghighi previously worked with Films Boutique on his 2018 comedy and Berlin competition title “Pig” and 2022 thriller “Subtraction,” which premiered at Toronto.

	A native of Tehran, the acclaimed director, screenwriter and actor has impressed with a cinematic style that “balances enigmatic storytelling, sociopolitical depth and formal experimentation,” Films Boutique noted.

schema.headline: Films Boutique Nabs Mani Haghighi’s ‘I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies’ Ahead of New York Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Fabien Frankel Joins Short Film ‘Love Unlimited’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Fabien Frankel, currently seen on screens as the dashing, honor-obsessed knight Ser Criston Cole in “House of the Dragon,” is ready to take on a ver
body:
Fabien Frankel, currently seen on screens as the dashing, honor-obsessed knight Ser Criston Cole in “House of the Dragon,” is ready to take on a very different role. 

	The British actor is set to star in “Love Unlimited,” the debut short drama from actor Olivier Huband (“A Discovery of Witches,” “Becoming Elizabeth”). Frankel will also serve as exec producer under his MarcelMonique Pictures banner, the company he runs with his brother Max Mark Frankel. Max Mark Frankel, who produced last year’s comedy feature “Our Hero, Balthasar,” will serve as lead producer on the project. 
	

	Written and directed by Huband, who also stars, “Love Unlimited” is described as a “small, sincere window into the profound, complex relationship between two old friends — Max (Frankel) and Gabriel (Huband) — as they unknowingly spend a final four days together in Max’s house in the South of France. The film exists in the world of the unspoken, exploring themes of male intimacy, grief and, as the title suggests, the incandescent, enduring power of love.”


	“Olivier sent me this script he had written about two best friends who spent their final summer together and we sat in my house and read it together and I found it immensely moving,” said Fabien Frankel, who as well as “House of Dragon” has also starred in “Task” and “The Serpent.” “It’s a subject incredibly close to my brother and I’s heart and we’re proud to get to be a part of it. It’s the first time I’ve acted in something I’ve produced so there are always some nerves that come with that, but I trust Olivier and my brother enough to guide us somewhere really special.”
	

	Huband produces with his sister Zara Huband under his Boneyard Films banner. Konstantin Mazov (“Coup de Grâce,” “Rokeby Venus”) has boarded the project as director of photography. Meanwhile, MarcelMonique Pictures have recruited the help of French production company All In Films, founded by Thomas Laget and Julien Floutard, to help bring the project to life.

	Production on  “Love Unlimited” is slated to start in September in the Pyrenees.

schema.headline: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Fabien Frankel Joins Short Film ‘Love Unlimited’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Pacifiction’ Director Albert Serra on His New Film ‘Sixteen Moments of My Life’ and Why He’d Love to Have Directed Elvis Presley
description: Don’t call Albert Serra’s new film, “Seize moments de ma vie” (“Sixteen Moments of My Life”), a concert film. Premiering out of competition at the L
body:
Don’t call Albert Serra’s new film, “Seize moments de ma vie” (“Sixteen Moments of My Life”), a concert film. Premiering out of competition at the Locarno Film Festival, the film documents a one-off performance by screen legend Ingrid Caven at the Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris. “I will never shoot a concert unless I’m involved in the music,” Serra told Variety. 

	The band were Molforts, the Catalan musicians who provide Serra’s soundtracks and Caven has been friends with the Spanish director for over fifteen years. Famed for her performances in the sixties and seventies of many European film classics as well as being the muse and frequent collaborator of her sometime husband, Rainer Werner Fassbinder, Caven is also a recording artist and Serra requested that they collaborate together with the musicians writing the music sending it over on CDs and Caven improvising over the music. 
	

	“Over the years the musicians and Caven wrote 16 songs, going back and forth. All this process, but they didn’t communicate directly. This is the point. They only communicate through the music itself. They didn’t talk.”


	Not so much the director as the MC? “I had all these things in front of me, I could hardly see the stage.” 

	This is how Serra also directs his films, such as “Liberté” and “Pacifiction.” “Everything is based on non-communication with the actors. I like when things happen without really working on meanings or on the outcome. Subconscious. Like old school Hollywood, you know, everybody has to do what they have to do, and we don’t need to discuss for hours. This was a similar concept.”
	

	The film continues Serra’s interest in performance. His last film, the documentary “Afternoons of Solitutde,” took as its subject a young and celebrated bullfighter and focused intently on him to the exclusion of everything else. So in “Sixteen Moments,” there are no cut-aways to the audience. “You have genius musicians on stage, and you want me to shoot some idiots watching them? No,” says Serra.

	The music is a mixture of autobiography sung in a way that drifts between opera, cabaret and Edith Piaff. At the very beginning we see Caven coughing before taking the stage. “Every performance is kind of life and death, and it’s unique: it’s fatality. Cinema is perfect for that, because cinema has the same logic. One moment of the film has passed, you cannot grab it, it’s passed. The experience of cinema, it’s the logic of live music or live performance. It has passed, and you cannot recover it. It’s very coherent with this fragility of creating musical life. You know that not everything is perfect. Not everything is under control always. And maybe this is part of the motion and the magic.”

	Having done a film on bullfighting and a singer, would there be another kind of performance he would like to document?

	“No, what would it be?” Serra says; then breaks into a grin. “I will do a musical comedy. This is something that has been a lot of times in my mind. I think I will end up doing it because I like this idea of musical comedy that’s positive. The spirit of something that is light: poetic and positive. Nowadays, with all this reality of the war and these problems and frictions and tensions and whatever, I’d like to make a “Brigadoon” style musical. Maximum happiness. The opposite of what I’ve been doing all of my life.”

	He also says that he wished he could’ve directed Maria Callas and Elvis Presley. “Elvis should have done dramatic roles, and with the right director, he would have been an amazing dramatic actor. And another idea I had was to make light comedies with Maria Callas, because she did only very very dramatic stuff with Pasolini. Very static like this opera and this intensity and this mythological stuff and very heavy. Why not make a comedy with her?” 

	It might not be boasting. Serra’s films have featured some iconic performances, such as Jean-Pierre Léaud as Louis XIV in “The Death of Louis XIV” and Benoît Magimel in “Pacifiction.” Of the latter, Serra says: “It’s the best performance of his career. Whatever people say: no, this is the best performance. I know it. I’m 100% sure.”
	

	From Wednesday, Serra is back in the editing suite working on his new film “Out of This World” which he hopes to have completed by the end of the year. “It’s 65% done.” 

	The film stars Riley Keough and F. Murray Abraham as part of an American delegation traveling to Russia in the context of the Ukraine war. “It’s not a war film, it’s about economics. You’ll see what happens in the film, where it goes at the end. It goes to the best scene of recent cinema. This I can tell you. So you will have to wait until the end.”

	That sounds like a headline. “Yes! And the second headline is ‘You will have to wait until the end.’”



	

					Albert Serra  Copyright: Oscar Fernández Orengo

title: ‘Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO’ Director Kamiyama Kenji Built His New Series Around a Metaphor for AI Fears: ‘Will We End Up Being Used by It?’
description: Kamiyama Kenji says the alien threat driving his new “Gundam” anime is a direct metaphor for humanity’s uneasy relationship with artificial intellig
body:
Kamiyama Kenji says the alien threat driving his new “Gundam” anime is a direct metaphor for humanity’s uneasy relationship with artificial intelligence. 

	The director, known for “Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex” and “The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim,” tells Variety he built “Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO” around that anxiety. 

	The series follows Ray Azumi (voiced by Takeo Otsuka), a war orphan who awakens on the lunar surface as the pilot of the experimental mobile suit Gundam ZERO. The story begins decades after humanity is forced to abandon Earth in the face of a hostile, self-replicating ecosystem born from an alien object’s three revelations: gravity control, faster-than-light communication and cognitive materialization. Humanity marks the years since in a calendar counted from that exile.
	

	Kamiyama explains why he placed Ray in a world where that exile is simply the everyday condition rather than a recent trauma: “As I explored, at the setting stage, the idea that this world too has a time ‘before today,’ I came to feel that rather than spelling out the setting from scratch, it would enrich the story more to let viewers imagine and fill in for themselves what came before today.”


	The new setting hinges on those three revelations turning catastrophic. Asked what that premise let him explore, Kamiyama says: “Can we truly master a technology we did not create ourselves, or will we end up being used by it? It is a metaphor for technologies that humanity is already beginning to struggle to handle in reality, such as AI.”

	When it comes to moving between giant, established mythologies like “Gundam,” “Star Wars” and Tolkien’s Middle-earth, Kamiyama strives to put his own spin on things while also staying true to what the fans want. “I try to prepare surprises while taking the utmost care not to stray from that consensus,” he says. “When that goes well, the sense of sharing the moment with the fans becomes the motivation to keep creating — that’s what I believe.”
	

	“Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO” also encompasses the companion video game, “Gundam Rogue Orbit.” “The project actually started from the game first, but the game side had no fixed setting in place, so I built out the world starting from the question of what Gundam fights,” Kamiyama says. He left the game’s mechanics to its own team, reasoning that “games have an appeal that only a game can deliver, the fun that comes from the gameplay and the controls.”

	To prepare a backstory for “Gundam Rogue Orbit,” Kamiyama had to work out what the monsters were, what they did to Earth and humanity, and how long it took for either side of the coming war to develop a countermeasure like Gundam. “Creating these fine details is, I’d say, both the hardest part and the real thrill of building a science fiction work,” he says.

	On what keeps pulling him back to stories about societies adapting to systems they can’t control, Kamiyama believes that “anti-war is a universal theme; even as the forms and meanings of war change with the times, it remains timeless.”

	He extends that idea to the current moment: “The true nature of war looks different from one era to the next. Perhaps it is the unease of the wars unfolding right now.” Building an era untethered from Gundam’s Universal Century or 00 timelines gave him that freedom, he says.

	On his approach to legacy IP after working with Tolkien and Lucasfilm’s properties, he says, “It was about choosing between what should be carried on and what should be built anew.”

	Kamiyama also reveals the scale of the world he has built beyond what “RG XARX-ZERO” itself shows. “At the very least, it stretches from 50 years before the point where this story begins to the start of another possible future that could connect to the game’s world 100 years later,” he says.

	For the science-fiction concepts underpinning that world, including gravity control, faster-than-light communication and cognitive materialization, Kamiyama worked with novelist Toh EnJoe, credited as SF setting supervisor, as an outside arbiter. “He is a master who rearranges words through mathematics, so whether or not to examine meaning became a source of creative inspiration,” Kamiyama says, describing EnJoe’s rulings on which ideas were plausible, needed more thought, or could be glossed over.
	

	Asked what he hopes is the first surprise for viewers meeting this world, Kamiyama says: “Gundam’s place within a body of work that has always had giant robots as its protagonists.”

	The director has spent two decades moving between franchises with devoted fan bases, from his breakout run steering “Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex” through its two seasons, to co-directing Netflix’s CG reboots of “Ultraman” and “Ghost in the Shell: SAC_2045” with Shinji Aramaki. His theatrical foray into Middle-earth with “The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim” reached screens worldwide in 2024, and he now oversees the “Star Wars: Visions” universe as supervising director on its 2026 installment, which extends the story he introduced in “The Ninth Jedi.”

	“Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO,” produced by Bandai Namco Filmworks with animation from Sola Animation, launches in 2027.

schema.headline: ‘Mobile Suit Gundam RG XARX-ZERO’ Director Kamiyama Kenji Built His New Series Around a Metaphor for AI Fears: ‘Will We End Up Being Used by It?’

title: ‘The Chosen’ Star Jonathan Roumie to Voice Banijay Live’s ‘Luminiscence’ Experience at St. Patrick’s Cathedral
description: Banijay is expanding its “Luminiscence” immersive experience franchise in the U.S. with an installation at New York’s iconic St. Patrick’s Cathedral
body:
Banijay is expanding its “Luminiscence” immersive experience franchise in the U.S. with an installation at New York’s iconic St. Patrick’s Cathedral that opens Oct. 1.

	To take viewers through the experience as narrator, the Banijay Live unit behind the “Luminiscence” business has tapped an actor who has logged more than a few miles in Jesus’ robes, Jonathan Roumie of “The Chosen” Bible-themed films and TV episodes.


	“Luminiscence” was created as an enveloping experience light, music and choral performances by comes to one of the U.S.’s most iconic spiritual addresses — on Manhattan’s Fifth Avenue — after drawing 2 million visitors across 20 productions in eight countries including France, Spain, the U.K., Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Brazil and smaller locations in the United States. The offerings at St. Patrick’s will vary as will ticket prices, depending on the extent of the experience.
	

	“Jonathan Roumie was the natural choice to lend his voice to ‘Luminiscence’ at St. Patrick’sCathedral in New York. His ability to bring authenticity, depth, and humanity to everyperformance makes him an ideal creative partner for an experience that invites audiences tostep inside the story in a deeply meaningful way,” said Ben Samek, CEO of Banijay Americas. “We’re building on an audience that already has a strong connection to this remarkable experience while creating a new way for them to engage with it.”

	Roumie said the work on “Luminiscence” at St. Patrick’s was meaningful to him as a “born-and-raised New Yorker.” The majestic structure “has always been a hallowed icon of faith, architecture and New York itself. Amidst the noisy grind of the city that refuses to sleep, one can find stillness, beauty, and peace among its graceful Gothic arches,” he said.
	

	“Luminiscence” was created by Lotchi, a unit of Banijay Live devoted to creating immersive experiences “designed to spark inspiration and wonder,” per the company. St. Patrick’s fits the bill nicely as North America’s largest Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral.

	“St. Patrick’s isn’t just a spectacular venue, it’s a place where generations of New Yorkers havegathered to celebrate and to hope, said Romain Sarfati, co-founder of Lotchi and creator of“Luminiscence.” “Every element of our show, the choir, the orchestra, the projections at themillimeter, is designed with that weight in mind. We’re not adding light to St. Patrick’s. We’re helping it reveal what’s already there.”

	Performances will run through the end of this year. Leaders of the beloved institution, including Ronald Hicks, Archbishop of New York, are eagerly anticipating the crowds that will be intrigued by the “Luminiscence” installation.

	“We are grateful for partners like ‘Luminiscence’ who share our commitment to caring for this historic space and inviting new generations to encounter it, be uplifted, and give glory to God – including the organ that has filled this Cathedral with music for nearly a century and that we are committed to preserving for a century more,” Hicks said.

schema.headline: ‘The Chosen’ Star Jonathan Roumie to Voice Banijay Live’s ‘Luminiscence’ Experience at St. Patrick’s Cathedral

title: RTL Group Posts 3.9% Revenue Rise as Streaming Side Grows, Though Fremantle Continues to Suffer
description: European media conglomerate RTL Group on Tuesday posted first-half figures showing strong growth in streaming, with revenue up 3.9% to €2.9 billion
body:
European media conglomerate RTL Group on Tuesday posted first-half figures showing strong growth in streaming, with revenue up 3.9% to €2.9 billion ($ 3.3 billion), while revenues from its linear TV side and its Fremantle content business were down.

	The acquisition of pay-TV operation ‌Sky Deutschland from Comcast in June has also increased the group’s revenue base. RTL said it now expects ​2026 revenue of €7.1 to €7.2 billion, ($8.20 ​billion-$8.32 billion), up from its previous ⁠forecast of €6.1 billion to €6.2 billion that it ​issued in March. 
	

	The deal will see Sky Deutschland merge with RTL+, creating a streaming platform with 12.4 million paid subscriptions across Germany, Austria and Switzerland. The company’s streaming operations also include M6+ in France.


	Adjusted EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization) was €239 million ($275 million) during the January-June period, up almost 50% from a year ​ago.

	“Our streaming businesses deliver strong profitability,” said RTL Group CEO Clément Schwebig in a statement. “Streaming revenue and paid subscriptions continue to grow dynamically. As a result, streaming is now expected to contribute around €100 million ($115 million) to our full-year operating profit,” he added. “We are now the clear No. 3 in the German-speaking streaming market,” Schwebig went on to note, calling the Sky Deutschland deal “transformational” for RTL.

	RTL’s streaming boost compensated for drops in its traditional TV business, where advertising revenue fell 4% while its production operations at Fremantle were down 7.7% year-on-year at $964 million (€835 million). But Schwebig said he expects a rise in Fremantle revenues by the year’s end with the rollout of new shows, including its “Baywatch” reboot that will debut in the U.S. on Fox in January 2027 and its thriller “Kill Jackie,” starring Catherine Zeta-Jones, which was acquired by HBO Max across key European markets ahead of its fall 2026 launch following earlier distribution deals with Prime Video and AMC+.
	

	“Fremantle will continue to invest significantly in IP development, in acquisitions of small and medium-sized production companies with a strong IP base and in the deployment of artificial intelligence across the company’s value chain,” Schwebig noted.

schema.headline: RTL Group Posts 3.9% Revenue Rise as Streaming Side Grows, Though Fremantle Continues to Suffer

title: Locarno: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Piluk,’ From the National Film Board of Canada, Discuss the Language of Animation
description: With a world premiere in the Locarno Film Festival‘s Pardi di Domani selection of short and medium-length films, the filmmakers behind “Piluk” saw t
body:
With a world premiere in the Locarno Film Festival‘s Pardi di Domani selection of short and medium-length films, the filmmakers behind “Piluk” saw the production as a chance to tell a story with the simplest possible textures: pencil, paper and the human voice. 

	Produced by Marc Bertrand and Jelena Popović of the National Film Board of Canada and directed by multidisciplinary artists and longtime friends Marc Séguin and Elisapie Isaac, “Piluk” was created from over 8,000 drawings using pen, charcoal and pencil and accompanied by a soundtrack of throat-singing.
	

	The National Film Board shared a clip of the short film with Variety:




	 “I have the most immense respect for things that can be said with pencil and paper,” Séguin says in an interview with Variety. “Given all the technology that surrounds us, I still think that not all has been said with paper and pencil. So we wanted to go back to that craftsmanship. I mean, if Eli’s on stage or she records something for this film, it’s her voice. We didn’t want machines to be involved or ask AI to get involved as well, we wanted to just draw it the old-fashioned way.”

	The story follows the journey of a girl called Piluk, born with wings on her back, as she crosses the countryside, eventually arriving at an unnamed city, caring for different animals along the way. There’s no dialogue: everything is communicated by its animation and by the expressive vocals of the choral soundtrack. The scratchy, sketchy linework goes for an impression of people and places rather than strictly realistic representation; the backgrounds mostly stripped away.
	



	

									Courtesy of the National Film Board of Canada
	



	Isaac says that the same principles applied to the soundtrack: the musician, being from an Inuk background, has spoken previously about taking inspiration from traditions of oral storytelling. Isaac says that at first she had been content to collaborate with Séguin in pre-production, but that “[when] it became clear that we’re not gonna overproduce, we’re not gonna over-add,” she began to want to experiment with the human voice. She enjoyed the sense of ambiguity to the way the voices mix with the imagery, that it feels organic this way, Isaac says. “We ended up keeping it very minimalist. What came out is just trying to respect what’s going on in the image and the world.”

	The idea of allowing room for audiences to project something of their own meaning was important for both the visuals and the soundtrack. “I think that was the purpose,” Isaac says of her approach to the music, “to leave space for people to feel.” To Isaac, lyrics and actual words or even “perfect melody” would be too structured; they wanted unpredictability.



	

									Courtesy of the National Film Board of Canada
	



	Though Séguin is renowned for his painting and has worked in filmmaking before (as has Isaac — the two have even collaborated before on projects such as Séguin’s 2016 feature “Stealing Alice”), producer Jelena Popović, who took over from Bertrand during the project, points out that both are new to animation as a medium.

	So it became part of NFB’s responsibility to support the artists in new territory, preserving their voice in the adaptation to working in a new format. This is, in Popović’s eyes, something inherent to NFB’s structure. “We are allies of the artist in a sense that we’re not profit driven, we’re a public money-funded producer and distributor,” she says. Making sure the artists can navigate this new space is but a small part of maintaining a sense of their influence over the story, something which extends to the NFB’s commitment to producing work by Indigenous artists.

	“The NFB obviously has a commitment to producing work by Indigenous storytellers and artists,” Popović says. “Many other indigenous artists work with the NFB, and hopefully we decolonize the institution through all of this work,” she adds, after listing works by artists such as Terril Calder, Jeff Barnaby and Walter Scott. “So in working with Elisapie and Marc, like any other filmmaker, and especially Indigenous filmmakers, it’s important to preserve this narrative sovereignty of the auteur. We are there to help! We are not there to prescribe anything nor impose anything.”
	

	The team of animators at the NFB studio was led by Parissa Mohit (“an amazing filmmaker and animator,” Popović says). “Parissa was their advisor for animation directing, and also the head of the animation team. These amazing exchanges, like the finessing of mise-en-scène and creating that illusion of movement, were really discussed in detail with Parissa and our technical director Eric Pouliot and the rest of our technical experts in-house.”

	Popović highlights the goal of supporting artists and helping them achieve their specific creative vision, describing NFB as a “creative laboratory.” “Artists come to us with an idea, and we give them a playground to explore in the development phase, and do many kinds of explorations [which] are really not easy to get in the private commercial sector,” Popović says. “We are not based on return on investment.” For Popović, who has also produced shorts such as “Hedgehog’s Home,” “Manivald” and “Bread Will Walk,” the film being made in the way the artists envisioned is the real return on investment — something which stems from a passion and belief in animation as “the sum and the summit of all arts with a capital A.”

	This is because, as Popović puts it, animation is “using the language of all the visual arts,” folding theater, drama and music into a cinematic language. “At the same time it’s an economical way of storytelling which is painstakingly long to make: you have to start from stereotypes and archetypes because that’s the language you know, and especially in short film animation, you have to adapt yourself to that economy of storytelling.” In their approach to “Piluk,” co-directors Séguin and Isaac have found just that kind of economy: finding the maximum emotional impact with the most minimal of art styles and musical instruments.



	

									Courtesy of the National Film Board of Canada

schema.headline: Locarno: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Piluk,’ From the National Film Board of Canada, Discuss the Language of Animation

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Battle Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office
description: Sony’s superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” retained its top spot at the U.K. and Ireland box office for a second consecutive week, tak
body:
Sony’s superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” retained its top spot at the U.K. and Ireland box office for a second consecutive week, taking £10.1 million ($13.6) over its sophomore frame. 

	The film’s cumulative total is now $87.4 million after 13 days of release.

	Universal’s epic “The Odyssey” held firm in second place during its fourth weekend of release. Directed by Christopher Nolan, the feature added $4.8 million, driving its running total to $82.6 million. 
	

	Paramount captured third place with the wide debut of animated feature “Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie,” which banked an opening frame of $2.2 million. Disney’s animated holdover “Toy Story 5” followed in fourth position in its eighth week, adding $848,063 to push its cume to $72.5 million. Universal’s “Minions & Monsters” completed the top five in its sixth week, taking $557,564 to raise its running total to $21.5 million.


	Piece Of Magic Entertainment claimed sixth spot with the specialized debut of “Andre Rieu’s 2026 Summer Concert: Viva Maastricht!,” drawing $671,742 across its event cinema rollout. Disney’s live-action “Moana” occupied seventh place in its fifth frame, generating $490,552 to drive its cume to $15.9 million.

	Studiocanal’s horror feature “Ice Cream Man” entered the chart in eighth place, recording an opening frame of $414,256. Black Bear’s comedy-drama “The Invite” captured ninth spot in its sixth week, adding $136,039 for a total of $5.1 million. Universal’s long-running horror-romance “Obsession” rounded out the top 10 in its 13th week of release, collecting $88,242 to lift its cume to $26.3 million.
	

	Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, Trafalgar is releasing Lee Kirk’s comedy “Nimrods: A Green Day Comedy” into more than 100 locations.

	Wide-circuit openings are led by Warner Bros.’ sci-fi survival drama “End Of Oak Street,” starring Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, True Brit Entertainment’s George Jaques-directed drama “Sunny Dancer” starring Bella Ramsey, and A24’s Tony Bourdain feature “Tony” starring Dominic Sessa and Antonio Banderas. 

	Broad rollouts include MetFilm’s Samuel Abrahams drama “Lady,” Munro’s Nat Boltt-directed drama “Holy Days,” Signature’s “Momo & The Time Thieves,” Reelistic Dreams’ “Never Had A Chance,” and Park Circus re-issuing Aardman’s animated comedy “The Pirates! In An Adventure With Scientists!”.

	Specialized and international counter-programming debuts include Mubi’s “Ancestral Visions of the Future,” Zee Studios International’s Tamil-language rom-com “Hi!,” Left Films’ “Mermaid Beach,” New Wave’s Venice-winning drama “Songs of Forgotten Trees,” and Dreamz Entertainment’s Telugu-language supernatural fantasy “Agadha”. The frame concludes with Source Entertainment launching Chris Atkins’ music documentary “James: Getting Away With It” across more than 100 locations.

            A rep for the San Diego PD tells us ... officers made the traffic stop on a vehicle carrying Blueface, Chrisean and their young son, Chrisean Jr., as they were apparently livestreaming Saturday night.  Blueface and the others had just left Blu Temple/Blu Cabana after the rapper had performed at the venue.
      
    
          Waiting for your permission to load TikTok Post.
      
    
            Cops said officers learned that someone in the vehicle was on probation, which, as part of the conditions of the court, required police to search the SUV for contraband. It's unclear who was on probation inside the vehicle.
      

            But police said no contraband was found, and the passengers and driver were eventually released without being arrested.

            Rep. Lauren Boebert’s son Tyler Boebert’s ex-girlfriend showed cops a 43-second video he filmed of her ... which led to his arrest for child sexual exploitation, TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            Per a criminal affidavit, 21-year-old Tyler, who was arrested on August 9, was charged with child sexual exploitation to induce or entice, possession with intent, sexual exploitation of a child, sexual exploitation of a child involving video, and two additional counts related to contributing to the delinquency of a minor.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The charges stem from an alleged video that a then-18-year-old Tyler filmed with his then-17-year-old girlfriend on April 1, 2024, who was reportedly turning 18 weeks after the video was shot. The ex-girlfriend reportedly called the police on April 2, 2024, after her ex was sent the video. 
      

            The affadavit also mentioned the alleged victim initially told the cops she was hesitant to report the incident ... because she didn't want Tyler to get in trouble.
      
    
            Tyler has yet to speak about the matter. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Rep. Boebert previously told TMZ, “I love my son.” 
      
    
            The politician added, “We take these allegations very seriously and pray for everyone affected during this challenging time." Tyler was released after posting a $10K bond. He will appear in court for a hearing later this month.

title: John Gotti's Grandson Enters Prison After Plan to Donate Kidney to Mom Ruined by Infection
description:
John Gotti's Grandson Carmine
                          Checks Into Prison
body:
John Gotti's Grandson Carmine
                          Checks Into Prison
                          After Failed Attempt to Give Mom a Kidney
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 11, 2026
                            5:28 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            John Gotti’s grandson Carmine Agnello has surrendered to the Bureau of Prisons after a New York judge denied his request to again delay his report date in order to donate his kidney to his ailing mom, Victoria Gotti.
      
    
            The BOP tells TMZ ... Carmine surrendered himself on Monday and is now housed at the Federal Correctional Institution (FCI) Fairton located in Fairton, New Jersey.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            We told you all about it -- Carmine was sentenced to 15 months in prison after pleading guilty in September 2024 to a $1.1 million wire fraud scheme tied to COVID-19 relief loans. He was able to secure an extension to his original July 20 report date due to his plans to donate a kidney to his sick mother.
      

            However, Victoria got a nasty infection just before they were both set to go under the knife on August 3 ... and the surgery was canceled. The judge overseeing the case gave Carmine until Aug. 10 to donate his kidney -- and if the kidney was donated by then, his surrender date would be pushed back to September 18 -- but Victoria was unable to get medically cleared for the surgery.
      
    
            Carmine's lawyer, Robert Beltrani, asked for a 3rd extension in a filing Monday ... but the judge denied, instead postponing Carmine's report time by 2 hours.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported Friday, sources connected to the Gotti family told TMZ this was an "emotional" time for them, adding the infection was an unforeseen issue, and Carmine simply wanted to help his mother as she battles severe kidney disease complications.
      
    
            They added Carmine was never trying to escape his sentence ... but wanted to secure the surgery before reporting to prison.
      
    
            TMZ has reached out to his attorney ... so far, no word back.
